questions.question: An internal agent for account managers can read CRM records, draft emails, update opportunities, and delete contacts. Account managers only ever read records and draft emails through it. Under least privilege, what is the right change?
options: Log every update and deletion for later audit
Add a confirmation dialog before updates and deletions
Restrict deletions to business hours
Remove the update and delete capabilities from the agent's configuration entirely
questions.explanation: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need, eliminating the attack and error surface rather than monitoring it. Logging (A) and confirmations (B) are compensating controls around a privilege that should not exist, and scheduling (C) narrows the window without closing it.

questions.question: After a nightly document refresh, your RAG assistant's answers turned confident but wrong. Model version, prompts, and latency are unchanged. Where do you look first?
options: The retrieval and indexing layer: whether the refresh broke the index, changed chunking, or introduced mismatched embeddings
The model, which may have degraded overnight
The system prompt wording
The temperature setting
questions.explanation: The only thing that changed is the document pipeline, and confident-but-wrong is the signature of plausible-but-irrelevant retrieved context. The pinned model (B), unchanged prompt (C), and sampling (D) do not correlate with the refresh.

questions.question: Your platform will expose forty internal capabilities to agents across many teams. Loading all forty tool definitions into every agent's context is bloating prompts and degrading tool selection. What is the architectural remedy?
options: Shorter tool descriptions across the board
Progressive discovery: agents load a small task-relevant toolset, with search or namespacing to pull in others when needed
One mega-tool with a mode parameter selecting among forty behaviors
Limit the platform to ten capabilities
questions.explanation: At large tool counts, progressive discovery beats monolithic context: each agent sees what its task needs. Uniformly terser descriptions (A) trade selection quality for tokens, a mode-switch mega-tool (C) hides forty behaviors from the selection mechanism entirely, and capping the platform (D) sacrifices the requirement.

questions.question: A bank wants a system that answers loan officers' policy questions with citations, and separately drafts decline letters from structured decision data. A vendor proposes one autonomous multi-agent system for both. What is the sounder architecture?
options: The proposed multi-agent system, since both tasks involve documents
One agent with all tools and a routing prompt
Two simple components: a retrieval-augmented answer service for policy questions, and a templated generation workflow for letters, each evaluated on its own metrics
A single fine-tuned model for both
questions.explanation: Two well-understood problems with different shapes deserve the two cheapest reliable structures, independently testable and governable. Shared document-ness (A) is not an architectural argument, one agent with everything (B) couples unrelated risk profiles, and fine-tuning (D) is the most expensive path to problems retrieval and templates already solve.

questions.question: Your architecture review board asks why you chose a deterministic workflow over an autonomous agent for claims intake. Which justification reflects the tested decision framework?
options: Agents are a newer pattern and less proven in general
Workflows always outperform agents
The team lacked time to build an agent
The intake path is fully known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, auditable, and reliable; autonomy earns its complexity only where the model must choose the path
questions.explanation: The framework is structural fit: known path, deterministic orchestration; open-ended path, agent. Novelty (A) and universal claims (B) are not engineering arguments, and resourcing (C) justifies a schedule, not an architecture.

questions.question: Legal review quality is subjective, and your team disagrees about whether the assistant's clause summaries are "good." What makes evaluation tractable?
options: Define a rubric with the failure modes that matter, build a labeled evaluation set with counsel, and combine rubric-based model grading with periodic human review
Ship and count complaints
Exact string match against one reference summary per clause
Grade outputs by length
questions.explanation: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology with humans anchoring the judgment. Complaint-counting (B) measures too late, exact match (C) fails every valid paraphrase, and length (D) measures nothing.

questions.question: A prompt change looks better in demos. Before rolling it to all users, what is the disciplined path?
options: Roll it out; demos are representative
Run it against the regression evaluation set, then A/B it against the current prompt on real traffic with predefined metrics before full rollout
Ask the team to vote
Roll out to everyone with a feedback banner
questions.explanation: Changes to prompts are production changes: regression evaluation catches breakage, and an A/B on defined metrics establishes improvement before exposure. Demos (A) and votes (C) are anecdotes, and full rollout with a banner (D) is the experiment without the control.

questions.question: A healthcare client requires that no protected health information reach the model provider, while clinicians want free-text queries about patients. Which design meets both?
options: Trust clinicians to avoid typing identifiers
A system prompt instructing the model to forget PHI
A de-identification layer that strips or tokenizes PHI before the API call, re-associating results locally, with logging and periodic audits of the boundary
Blocking free-text queries entirely
questions.explanation: Compliance boundaries are enforced by architecture: PHI is removed before it crosses, and the control is auditable. Trust (A) is not a control, model instructions (B) act after the data already crossed, and a hard block (D) fails the stated business need that a compliant design can meet.

questions.question: Your Claude solution's executive sponsor asks for "99.9% accuracy or we cancel." Accuracy on the task plateaus near 92% with human review catching the rest. What is the architect's correct move?
options: Promise 99.9% and hope model upgrades close the gap
Decline to discuss numbers with non-engineers
Quietly redefine accuracy so the number reads higher
Reframe the target around the end-to-end process: the system plus confidence-routed human review achieves the business outcome, with measured rates, costs, and the tradeoff curve made explicit
questions.explanation: Managing expectations with explicit, honest tradeoffs is scored material at this level: the deliverable is the business outcome of the whole pipeline, not a raw model metric. Overpromising (A), stonewalling (B), and metric games (C) each destroy the trust the role exists to build.

questions.question: Three teams configure Claude Code independently: conventions drift, and new engineers take days to become productive. What is the enablement fix?
options: Ship a shared baseline: version-controlled team configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path, with team-specific rules layered on top
Mandate that engineers memorize the conventions
Prohibit Claude Code until conventions settle
Let each engineer keep personal settings only
questions.explanation: Team-level enablement means shared, versioned configuration with local extension, which is what makes tooling productive at organizational scale. Memorization (B) does not configure anything, prohibition (C) discards the productivity the domain exists to deliver, and personal-only settings (D) is the drift you started with.

questions.question: A customer requires that no request data leave their AWS account. Which deployment satisfies the constraint?
options: The Claude API with a signed data processing agreement
Claude through Amazon Bedrock within the customer's own account and region
The Claude API with request logging disabled
Any deployment, provided the data is encrypted in transit
questions.explanation: A residency constraint of this kind is met by running within the customer's own cloud boundary, which is what Bedrock provides. A contractual agreement (A), disabled logging (C), and transport encryption (D) all still involve the data leaving the account.

questions.question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud and requires identity, billing, and audit to run through existing controls. What follows?
options: Deploy on Bedrock for feature parity
Use the Claude API and replicate the controls
Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
Let each team choose its own path
questions.explanation: Aligning with the platform the enterprise already governs is what makes existing controls apply without duplication. A different cloud (A) creates a second control plane, replication (B) is expensive and drifts, and per-team choice (D) removes governance.

questions.question: A design places Claude behind an internal service that every application calls. What is the principal benefit?
options: It reduces token cost
It removes the need for evaluation
It guarantees lower latency
Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and model routing are enforced in one place
questions.explanation: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns can be applied consistently and changed once. It does not reduce token cost (A) or remove the need to evaluate (B), and an extra hop generally adds latency (C).

questions.question: A legacy system can only call synchronous endpoints with a two-second timeout, but the task needs long reasoning. What is the appropriate design?
options: Accept the request, return an identifier immediately, and deliver the result asynchronously
Force the model to answer within two seconds
Increase the legacy timeout
Use the smallest model available
questions.explanation: Decoupling submission from delivery lets the constraint and the workload coexist without degrading either. Truncating the reasoning (B, D) sacrifices the task, and changing the legacy system (C) is usually the constraint rather than an option.

questions.question: What is the most important consideration when a solution must run across two clouds?
options: Using identical prompts in both
Establishing which behaviors must be identical and evaluating for those on each platform
Choosing the cheaper platform for both
Deploying to whichever region is nearest
questions.explanation: Cross-platform equivalence is a requirement to be defined and then verified, not assumed. Identical prompts (A) do not guarantee identical behavior, and cost (C) and proximity (D) do not address consistency.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks for an autonomous agent to handle an end-to-end financial approval process. What should the architect establish first?
options: Which model to use
The expected token cost
Which decisions carry accountability and must remain with a person
Whether the agent can be built in the available time
questions.explanation: Where accountability sits determines the shape of the solution and what may be automated at all. Model choice (A), cost (B), and schedule (D) are all downstream of that boundary.

questions.question: Two designs meet the functional requirement. One is simpler and slightly less capable. What should decide?
options: The more capable design, since capability is the point
The design the team finds more interesting
The design with more components, for future flexibility
Whether the extra capability is needed by a stated requirement, weighed against the cost of complexity
questions.explanation: Complexity is a cost paid continuously in operation and maintenance, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Capability for its own sake (A), preference (B), and speculative flexibility (C) all pay that cost without justification.

questions.question: A proposed architecture depends on the model behaving correctly for a control that regulation requires. What is the correct judgment?
options: Unacceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
Acceptable if evaluation shows high accuracy
Acceptable with a disclaimer to the regulator
Acceptable if a larger model is used
questions.explanation: A regulatory control needs a guarantee, and probabilistic behavior cannot supply one however high the measured accuracy. Accuracy (B), disclosure (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee.

questions.question: What is the clearest sign that a solution has been over-engineered?
options: It uses more than one model
Components exist that no stated requirement depends on
It has an evaluation suite
It includes a human approval step
questions.explanation: Unjustified components are the definition of over-engineering and are the parts that will rot. Multiple models (A), evaluation (C), and approval steps (D) are all defensible when a requirement calls for them.

questions.question: What must exist before a solution can be said to be ready for production?
options: A demonstration that impressed stakeholders
Agreement from the engineering team
A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
A completed cost estimate
questions.explanation: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar, which is what distinguishes it from an impression. Demonstrations (A), consensus (B), and cost (D) do not establish whether the system works.

questions.question: An evaluation set is drawn entirely from cases the system already handles well. What is the consequence?
options: It gives a reliable measure of quality
It is acceptable if it is large enough
It only matters for regulated systems
It overstates performance and hides the failure modes that matter
questions.explanation: An unrepresentative set measures the wrong distribution, and size cannot correct a biased sample. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix bias (B), and the problem is universal rather than sector-specific (C).

questions.question: A prompt change improves the target metric but degrades an unmeasured behavior. How is this best prevented?
options: Maintaining a regression suite that covers behaviors the system must not lose
Changing one thing at a time
Reviewing changes more carefully
Limiting how often prompts change
questions.explanation: Silent regressions are caught by explicitly testing what must not break. Single changes (B) and careful review (C) reduce risk without detecting it, and slowing change (D) does not make it safe.

questions.question: What should trigger re-evaluation of a deployed solution?
options: Only a reported incident
A change to the model, the prompt, the data distribution, or the requirement
A fixed annual schedule
A change in cost
questions.explanation: Any change to the things that determine behavior invalidates prior measurement. Waiting for incidents (A) detects late, a fixed schedule (C) is unrelated to actual change, and cost (D) does not affect correctness.

questions.question: How should an architect treat a request to log full prompts and responses for audit?
options: Implement it, since audit requirements take precedence
Refuse, since logging creates risk
Establish what the audit actually requires, since prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data
Log responses only
questions.explanation: Audit and data protection are both real constraints, and the design must satisfy the audit purpose without retaining more than is warranted. Blanket implementation (A) and blanket refusal (B) ignore one side, and a partial rule (D) is arbitrary without knowing the requirement.

questions.question: What is the correct treatment of content retrieved from an untrusted source before it reaches the model?
options: It is safe once scanned for known attack strings
It is safe if the model is instructed to disregard instructions within it
It is safe if it comes over an encrypted channel
It is untrusted data throughout, and the model's authority must be bounded regardless of its content
questions.explanation: The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its permissions whatever the content persuades it to attempt. String scanning (A) and prompt instructions (B) are bypassable, and transport security (C) says nothing about the content.

questions.question: Who is accountable for a wrong decision produced by an automated Claude workflow?
options: The organization that deployed the workflow
The model provider
The engineer who wrote the prompt
Nobody, since the output was automated
questions.explanation: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes, which is why the boundaries of automation are an architectural decision. The provider (B) supplies a capability, individual authorship (C) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D).

questions.question: An executive sponsor asks for a single number showing how good the solution is. What is the right response?
options: Provide the headline accuracy figure
Provide the measure that matches the decision they face, with its limits stated
Explain that quality cannot be summarised
Provide the model's benchmark score
questions.explanation: A useful metric is one tied to the decision at hand and honest about what it does not cover. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark score (D) can mislead, and refusing to summarise (C) fails the sponsor.

questions.question: A pilot succeeded with ten users and the business wants to roll out to two thousand. What should the architect raise first?
options: The cost of additional licenses
The need for a larger model
Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
The training schedule
questions.explanation: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and naming those is the architect's contribution. Licenses (A), model size (B), and training (D) are downstream of knowing what breaks.

questions.question: What most reduces the risk that a delivered solution decays after handover?
options: Full documentation at delivery
A longer warranty period
Training every user
A named owner with a defined routine for evaluation, monitoring, and update
questions.explanation: Decay is prevented by ongoing ownership and a routine, not by artefacts produced once. Documentation (A) and training (C) age, and a warranty (B) covers defects rather than drift.

questions.question: How should an architect choose a model for a solution with several different tasks?
options: Match each task to the smallest model that meets its requirement, and evaluate the choices
One model for everything, for simplicity
The largest model for everything, for safety
The newest model for everything
questions.explanation: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate while evidence supports the choice. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit.

questions.question: What is the correct treatment of the context window in a production design?
options: A capacity to fill as fully as possible
A budget to allocate deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
A limit that only matters for long documents
A setting to raise when quality drops
questions.explanation: Context is a scarce resource whose allocation determines quality, so it is designed rather than consumed. Filling it (A) invites dilution, it matters well beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix an allocation problem.

questions.question: A solution's prompts are maintained by three teams and have diverged. What is the appropriate remedy?
options: Appoint one team to own all prompting
Freeze the prompts
Version the prompts as artefacts with defined ownership, review, and evaluation on change
Move all prompts into the system prompt
questions.explanation: Prompts that determine production behavior deserve the same lifecycle as code. Centralising ownership (A) may not fit the organization, freezing (B) blocks improvement, and relocation (D) does not address governance.

questions.question: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across many repositories. What is the most durable approach?
options: A written policy circulated by email
A one-off training session
Requiring approval for each use
Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code
questions.explanation: Conventions travel when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (C) creates friction without conveying practice.

questions.question: What is the most useful measure of whether a developer enablement program is working?
options: Change in the outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
The number of people trained
License utilization
The volume of tool calls
questions.explanation: Enablement is justified by the outcome it moves, which is what should be measured. Attendance (B), utilization (C), and activity (D) measure uptake rather than benefit.

questions.question: A team reports that Claude Code helps with new code but hurts on a legacy service. What should the architect investigate?
options: Whether the team needs more training
Whether the legacy service lacks the committed context and conventions the model needs
Whether a larger model would help
Whether the legacy service should be rewritten
questions.explanation: A difference between codebases usually reflects a difference in the context available in each. Training (A) does not supply repository context, a larger model (C) cannot infer undocumented conventions, and a rewrite (D) is a disproportionate response to a diagnosis not yet made.

questions.question: A retailer wants Claude to answer product questions from a 40,000-document catalog that changes daily. Which architecture fits?
options: Fine-tune a model on the catalog nightly
Load the catalog into the system prompt
Retrieval over an index refreshed as the catalog changes, with the model answering from retrieved context
An autonomous agent that browses the public website
questions.explanation: Frequently changing knowledge belongs in retrieval, not in weights or a context window

questions.question: After a re-index, your retrieval system returns semantically similar but commercially wrong products. Which investigation comes first?
options: The generation prompt
The model version
The user interface
Chunking and embedding configuration, and whether the index was rebuilt consistently
questions.explanation: Degradation following a re-index points at chunking, embeddings, and index consistency

questions.question: An agent used by 300 employees exposes 45 tools across eight systems. Selection quality is degrading. What is the architectural response?
options: Scope toolsets per task or role, with progressive discovery for the rest
Shorten all tool descriptions
Merge tools into a few multi-mode tools
Replace the agent with a larger model
questions.explanation: At large tool counts, scoping and progressive discovery preserve selection quality

questions.question: Which evaluation design best fits a summarization feature where quality is subjective?
options: Exact match against reference summaries
A rubric covering the failure modes that matter, applied by model graders and periodically audited by humans on a labeled set
Average output length compared to references
User thumbs-up counts alone
questions.explanation: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology

questions.question: Before a prompt change reaches all users, what is the disciplined sequence?
options: Ship it and monitor complaints
Team vote followed by rollout
Regression evaluation, then a controlled A/B against the current prompt on predefined metrics, then rollout
Rollout with a feedback form
questions.explanation: Prompt changes are production changes: regression first, then a controlled comparison

questions.question: A hospital system requires that protected health information never reach the model provider, while clinicians need free-text search. Which design satisfies both?
options: A policy instructing clinicians not to type identifiers
A system prompt instructing the model to disregard PHI
Restricting the feature to structured queries only
A de-identification layer that removes or tokenizes PHI before the call, with local re-association and auditing
questions.explanation: Compliance boundaries are enforced architecturally before data crosses, and audited

questions.question: Which is the correct application of human-in-the-loop review at scale?
options: Route by confidence and consequence, so low-confidence and high-impact cases reach humans while routine cases flow through
Review every output regardless of risk
Review a fixed 10% sample chosen at random
Review only what users complain about
questions.explanation: Confidence and consequence routing makes human review affordable and effective

questions.question: An executive sponsor demands a single accuracy number for a system whose performance varies sharply by document type. What does a competent architect present?
options: The highest observed number
Performance broken out by document type with the aggregate, the measurement method, and what the business outcome is after human review
A refusal to quantify
An average weighted to look favorable
questions.explanation: Honest segmentation plus method and end-to-end outcome is what earns and keeps trust

questions.question: Your design must satisfy GDPR for EU customer data. Which requirement most directly shapes the architecture?
options: Response latency targets
The choice of programming language
Data minimization, purpose limitation, and the ability to delete personal data on request
The number of model providers
questions.explanation: GDPR drives minimization, purpose limitation, and erasure, all of which shape design

questions.question: Which is the correct reason to prefer a workflow over an agent for a document intake process?
options: Workflows are always more accurate
Agents cannot process documents
Workflows use less context
The processing path is known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable, and auditable
questions.explanation: Known path, deterministic orchestration; autonomy earns its complexity only when the path is not known

questions.question: An application sends an identical 12,000-token policy preamble on every request. Which optimization addresses both latency and cost?
options: Ordering the static preamble first and enabling prompt caching
Splitting the preamble across two requests
Summarizing the preamble with the model at request time
Moving the preamble into a few-shot block
questions.explanation: A stable cached prefix cuts time-to-first-token and per-request cost together

questions.question: What belongs in an architecture decision record for a Claude system?
options: The final design only
The decision, the alternatives considered, the tradeoffs, and the constraints that drove the choice
The team members involved
The implementation timeline
questions.explanation: A decision record captures alternatives and tradeoffs, not just the outcome

questions.question: Observability for a production agent should capture which of the following to make incidents diagnosable?
options: Final outputs only
Aggregate latency metrics only
Traces of tool calls, retrieved context, and decision points alongside outputs
User feedback only
questions.explanation: Without traces of tool calls and retrieved context, failures cannot be localized to a layer

questions.question: A partner team wants to adopt your Claude Code setup. What makes adoption durable rather than a one-time handoff?
options: A recorded walkthrough
A shared chat channel
Individual coaching sessions
Version-controlled shared configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path that new engineers follow
questions.explanation: Shared, versioned configuration with an onboarding path is what makes adoption stick

questions.question: Which change best reduces risk in an agent that can both read and modify production records?
options: Separating read and write capabilities, granting write access only where the role requires it, and gating writes behind explicit approval
Logging modifications for later review
Requiring a longer system prompt about caution
Running the agent during business hours only
questions.explanation: Least privilege plus approval gates on writes reduces the surface rather than monitoring it

questions.question: A client requires that inference run inside their own AWS account. What does this determine?
options: The model family only
That a data processing agreement is sufficient
Deployment through Amazon Bedrock in the client's account and region
That request logging must be disabled
questions.explanation: Running inside the client's own cloud boundary is what the requirement describes. A contract (B) and logging settings (D) do not keep the data in the account, and the model family (A) is a separate choice

questions.question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud wants identity and audit handled by existing controls. What follows?
options: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
Use the Claude API and rebuild the controls
Use Bedrock for feature parity
Let each team decide
questions.explanation: Aligning with the governed platform makes existing controls apply without duplication. Rebuilding (B) drifts, a different cloud (C) creates a second control plane, and per-team choice (D) removes governance

questions.question: What is the main architectural benefit of routing all model traffic through one internal service?
options: Lower token prices
It removes the need for evaluation
It guarantees lower latency
Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and routing are applied consistently in one place
questions.explanation: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns are enforced and changed once. It does not change unit price (A), remove evaluation (B), or reduce latency (C)

questions.question: Two designs both satisfy the requirement; one is materially simpler. What decides?
options: The more capable design, since headroom is valuable
Whether any stated requirement needs the extra capability, against the ongoing cost of complexity
Whichever the team prefers to build
The one with more components, for flexibility
questions.explanation: Complexity is paid for continuously, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Headroom (A), preference (C), and speculative flexibility (D) pay that cost without justification

questions.question: A required compliance control depends on the model behaving correctly. What is the correct judgment?
options: Acceptable if measured accuracy is very high
Not acceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
Acceptable with a documented residual risk
Acceptable if a larger model is used
questions.explanation: A control that must hold needs a guarantee, which probabilistic behavior cannot supply. High accuracy (A), documentation (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee

questions.question: Where should the boundary of automation be drawn in a solution that makes customer-affecting decisions?
options: Wherever the model performs well in testing
As far as the budget allows
At whatever the client requests
Where accountability for the decision sits, keeping those decisions with a person
questions.explanation: Accountability determines what may be automated at all, and that boundary is an architectural decision. Test performance (A), budget (B), and unexamined requests (C) do not address responsibility

questions.question: What must exist before a solution is declared production-ready?
options: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
A successful demonstration
Sign-off from the engineering team
A completed cost model
questions.explanation: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar. A demonstration (B), consensus (C), and cost (D) do not establish whether it works

questions.question: An evaluation set contains only cases the system already handles. What is the effect?
options: It provides a reliable quality measure
It is fine if it is large
It overstates performance and conceals the failures that matter
It matters only in regulated contexts
questions.explanation: An unrepresentative sample measures the wrong distribution, and size does not correct bias. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix it (B), and the problem is general (D)

questions.question: How should a request to log every prompt and response for audit be handled?
options: Implement it, since audit takes precedence
Decline, because logging creates risk
Log responses but not prompts
Establish what the audit requires, because prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data
questions.explanation: Audit and data protection are both real, and the design must serve the audit purpose without retaining more than warranted. Blanket action (A) or refusal (B) ignores one side, and an arbitrary split (C) is unjustified

questions.question: Who is accountable when an automated Claude workflow produces a harmful decision?
options: The model provider
The engineer who wrote the prompt
The organization that deployed it
No one, because the decision was automated
questions.explanation: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes. The provider (A) supplies a capability, individual authorship (B) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D)

questions.question: A sponsor asks for one number that shows whether the solution is working. What is the right response?
options: Give the headline accuracy figure
Give the measure tied to the decision they face, and state what it does not cover
Explain that this cannot be reduced to a number
Give the model's benchmark score
questions.explanation: A useful metric matches the decision and is honest about its limits. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark (D) can mislead, and refusing (C) fails the sponsor

questions.question: A ten-user pilot is about to expand to two thousand users. What should the architect raise first?
options: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
License cost
Whether a larger model is needed
The training rollout plan
questions.explanation: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and surfacing those is the architect's contribution. Cost (B), model size (C), and training (D) follow from knowing what breaks

questions.question: How should a model be chosen for a solution containing several distinct tasks?
options: Match each task to the smallest model meeting its requirement, and evaluate the choices
One model everywhere, for simplicity
The largest model everywhere, for safety
The newest model everywhere
questions.explanation: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate on evidence. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit

questions.question: How should the context window be treated in a production design?
options: As capacity to fill as completely as possible
As a budget allocated deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
As a concern only for long documents
As a setting to increase whenever quality drops
questions.explanation: Context is scarce and its allocation drives quality, so it is designed. Filling it (A) dilutes, it matters beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix allocation

questions.question: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across dozens of repositories. What is most durable?
options: A policy document circulated once
A single training session
Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code
Requiring approval for every use
questions.explanation: Conventions persist when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (D) adds friction without conveying practice

questions.question: A client will not accept a solution whose behavior cannot be explained to their auditor. What does this constrain?
options: The model family only
The cost model
The architecture, which must make decisions traceable and the controls inspectable
The deployment region
questions.explanation: Auditability is an architectural property covering tracing and inspectable controls. Model family (A), cost (B), and region (D) do not by themselves make behavior explicable

questions.question: What is the main risk of building directly against a single cloud's model service with no abstraction?
options: Moving later becomes expensive, because the coupling reaches into application code
Higher token cost
Lower accuracy
Slower responses
questions.explanation: Coupling determines the cost of change, which is the architectural concern. Cost (B), accuracy (C), and latency (D) are not consequences of the coupling itself

questions.question: A solution must serve users in two regions with different data residency rules. What follows?
options: One deployment in the cheaper region
A single deployment with encryption in transit
Whichever region has the lowest latency
Separate deployments whose data stays within each region's boundary
questions.explanation: Residency is satisfied by keeping the data within each boundary. A single deployment (A, B) moves data across it, and latency (C) does not address the rule

questions.question: A requirement is stated as make it as accurate as possible. What should the architect do?
options: Choose the largest model and optimise from there
Establish the accuracy the use case actually needs and what an error costs
Build the most complex design the budget allows
Defer the question until after the pilot
questions.explanation: An unbounded requirement cannot be designed against or verified, so it must be made concrete. Defaulting to maximum capability (A, C) spends without a target, and deferring (D) leaves the design unanchored

questions.question: Two components each work correctly but the system fails intermittently at their boundary. What does this suggest?
options: One component needs a larger model
The contract between them is underspecified, particularly for edge and error cases
The system needs more components
The failure is transient and can be retried
questions.explanation: Boundary failures between correct components point at the contract. Capability (A) and more components (C) do not define the interface, and retrying (D) hides it

questions.question: A design proposes storing every model interaction indefinitely. What should the architect raise?
options: Nothing, retention is always safer
That storage is expensive
That it will slow the system
Why the data is needed, for how long, and what obligations retention creates
questions.explanation: Retention creates obligations and risk, so purpose and duration must justify it. Treating retention as free of risk (A) is the error, and cost (B) and speed (C) are minor by comparison

questions.question: How should a solution handle the case where the model is confident and wrong?
options: Design so that consequential outputs are verified against something independent of the model
Trust the confidence signal
Ask the model to double-check
Use two models and take the agreement
questions.explanation: Independence is what catches confident error. Confidence (B) is not evidence, self-checking (C) is not independent, and two models can agree and both be wrong (D)

questions.question: An evaluation shows 94% accuracy. What else must be known before this is actionable?
options: The model version only
The token cost of the evaluation
What the 6% look like, and what each failure costs
How long the evaluation took
questions.explanation: A headline rate is only meaningful alongside the shape and cost of the failures. Version (A), cost (B), and duration (D) do not describe the risk

questions.question: What should happen when a model version is updated beneath a production solution?
options: Nothing, versions are compatible
Increase monitoring for a week
Roll back automatically if complaints rise
Re-run the evaluation suite before the change reaches production traffic
questions.explanation: A change to the thing that determines behavior invalidates prior measurement. Assuming compatibility (A) is unsafe, and monitoring (B) or reacting to complaints (C) detects after users are affected

questions.question: A stakeholder asks why the solution cannot simply be fully automated. What is the most useful answer?
options: That the technology is not ready
That automation is always risky
Which specific decisions carry accountability or are unverifiable, and what automating them would risk
That the budget does not allow it
questions.explanation: A specific, reasoned boundary is actionable and can be revisited. Generic claims about readiness (A) or risk (B) are not, and budget (D) is not the reason

questions.question: What should be handed over with a solution so it survives its first year?
options: The source code
The evaluation suite, the criteria, the owner, and the routine for re-checking
A recorded demonstration
A list of prompts used
questions.explanation: Continuity depends on being able to measure and maintain, with someone responsible. Code (A), a demonstration (C), and prompts (D) are artefacts without the means to verify them

questions.question: A team reports the solution has become worse, but nothing was deployed. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The inputs or the surrounding usage changed
The model degraded on its own
The prompts wore out
The evaluation was wrong originally
questions.explanation: Behavior changes with what is fed to it, and distribution drift is the usual cause. Models do not degrade unprompted (B), prompts do not wear out (C), and the original evaluation is not the first suspect (D)

questions.question: How should prompts that determine production behavior be managed?
options: Versioned, owned, reviewed, and evaluated on change, like code
Edited in place when someone notices a problem
Kept in a shared document for easy editing
Frozen after launch
questions.explanation: Anything that determines production behavior needs the lifecycle of code. Ad hoc edits (B) and open documents (C) invite unreviewed change, and freezing (D) blocks improvement

questions.question: An organization asks how to measure whether Claude Code is worth the license cost. What should be measured?
options: Number of tool invocations
Change in the delivery outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
Number of users onboarded
Hours spent in the tool
questions.explanation: Value is the outcome moved, not the activity generated. Invocations (A), onboarding (C), and time in tool (D) measure usage rather than benefit

questions.question: What most often blocks a team from getting good results from Claude Code on an existing codebase?
options: The size of the repository
The programming language
The absence of committed context describing the conventions and structure
The number of contributors
questions.explanation: Missing project context is the usual cause, and it is the one the team can fix. Size (A), language (B), and contributor count (D) do not by themselves prevent good results

questions.question: You are designing an agent that can modify customer records. Where do approval gates and audit trails belong?
options: In the system prompt, with instructions to confirm before writing and to summarize every action at the end of each run
In the observability stack, with traces sampled at 10% and reviewed in a weekly governance meeting
In a post-launch hardening phase, once task completion is stable enough to show which code paths actually matter
In the tool layer from the start, with a log per tool call and an approval gate on every irreversible write
questions.explanation: Gates and logging enforced in the tool layer cover every path the model can take, and they are cheapest to design in at the start. Prompt instructions to confirm are advisory and can be skipped under pressure; sampled traces miss most actions; governance bolted on afterwards misses paths.

questions.question: How do you decide which tools an autonomous agent may call without a person?
options: Classify each action by blast radius: read-only and reversible calls run freely, irreversible or external ones need approval
Allow every tool inside the agent's own sandbox and require approval only for calls that cross a network boundary
Let the model rate the risk of each call itself and request approval whenever its stated confidence falls below a configured threshold
Gate every tool at launch and remove the gate from whichever tools users approve most often during the first month
questions.explanation: Classify actions by what happens if they are wrong: reversibility and reach decide the gate. A network boundary is the wrong proxy, since a local delete is just as irreversible as a remote one, and approval frequency measures convenience rather than risk.

questions.question: A client engagement involves personal data. What must the architecture cover beyond the model calls?
options: Encryption at rest and in transit for every store the agent touches, with keys held in the client's own key management service
A data processing agreement with the model provider plus a zero-retention setting on the API organization
Retention limits, PII redaction where possible, isolation from other clients' data, and access control on the logs
An anonymized eval set so that test runs and CI pipelines contain no real customer records or identifiers
questions.explanation: Data handling is part of the system: retention, minimization, isolation, and who can read the logs. Encryption is necessary but says nothing about how long data is kept or who can read it, and a provider agreement covers the provider's side, not your own logs and stores.

questions.question: An executive asks whether to fund the agent system. What framing lands?
options: The eval harness design, benchmark scores against the previous model, and the token budget per task
Cost per completed task, measured reliability, the known failure modes, how each is caught, and what fixing them takes
The architecture diagram, the tool inventory, and the prompt techniques that produced the accuracy gains
A live demo of the happy path with a projection of headcount savings once the agent reaches full autonomy
questions.explanation: Executives fund outcomes and risks they can reason about: cost, reliability, failure modes, and recovery. A happy-path demo with a savings projection hides exactly the failure and recovery information that decides whether the investment is sound.

questions.question: A new model version is available. What is the responsible upgrade path for a production agent?
options: Run the golden eval set on the new model, compare against the current baseline, then roll out gradually with monitoring
Pin the current model until the provider's deprecation date, then switch in one release with a rollback tag ready
Point staging at the new model on release day and promote to production after a week with no complaints from the engineers using it
Run the new model in shadow mode on live traffic for a quarter and adopt it only if no user reports a regression
questions.explanation: Upgrades are lifecycle events: evaluate, compare, canary, monitor. A quarter of shadow traffic is slow and relies on user reports rather than measurement; a week of informal staging use has no baseline to compare against.

questions.question: Which metrics tell you a production agent is drifting?
options: Token volume per day, API error codes, and the number of prompt versions shipped in the quarter
Uptime of the agent service, p99 latency of the model endpoint, and the provider's status page history
Ticket volume from users, time to first response from the team, and the count of open bugs tagged to the agent
Tool error rate, cost per completed task, latency, and eval scores tracked over time
questions.explanation: Operational signals tracked over time show drift before users complain. Uptime and endpoint latency describe availability, not quality, and user ticket volume is a lagging signal that arrives after the drift has done damage.

questions.question: A multi-agent system fails in cascades when one worker misbehaves. What architectural controls apply?
options: Redundant workers per task with majority voting, so a single misbehaving worker is outvoted by the others
A larger context window for the coordinator so it can hold every worker transcript and spot problems itself
Timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers per worker, and a coordinator that can stop the run
Stricter output schemas and a shorter system prompt per worker, reducing the chance that any worker misbehaves
questions.explanation: Limits and a coordinator that can halt the run are what contain cascading failures. Voting adds workers and cost without a way to stop a run that is going wrong, and prevention through stricter schemas does not contain the failures that still occur.

questions.question: Prompts are edited by several engineers and quality varies release to release. What fixes the process?
options: Assign one owner per prompt who approves edits by hand and keeps a changelog in the team wiki
Version prompts in source control with review, and run the eval set in CI on every change
Freeze the prompts for a quarter at a time and batch all edits into a single tested release
Move the variable parts of each prompt into a config service so engineers edit settings rather than prose
questions.explanation: Treat prompts like code: versioned, reviewed, and tested automatically. A single human approver adds a bottleneck without measurement, and a config service changes where edits happen without testing their effect.

questions.question: When should a deployed agent system be retired?
options: When the model it was built on is deprecated, since a migration costs about as much as a rebuild
When its eval scores fall below the launch baseline for two consecutive review periods
When the original sponsor leaves and no team is willing to take over on-call for it
When its measured value no longer covers cost and upkeep, and a simpler alternative covers the need
questions.explanation: Lifecycle management includes the end: measure value against cost and decommission on evidence. Falling eval scores call for a fix or a rollback, not retirement, and a model deprecation is a migration event rather than a reason to stop delivering value.

questions.question: A stakeholder wants "an agent for everything". What do you establish before building?
options: Success metrics, the tasks in scope, and which decisions stay with people
The full tool inventory the agent would need and the MCP servers that expose each system
A pilot with the widest possible scope so that real usage reveals which tasks are worth keeping
The model tier, the token budget per task, and the evaluation harness for the first release
questions.explanation: Scope and metrics first. Without them there is nothing to evaluate against and no way to say no. A wide pilot defers the scoping decision to usage data that nobody has defined how to judge, and tool inventories follow from scope rather than preceding it.

questions.question: A multi-agent system has a planner, three workers, and a verifier. The verifier rejects 40% of worker output. Where do you look first?
options: The verifier's rubric, since a strict rubric applied to reasonable output is the more common cause of a high rejection rate in practice
The worker model tier, since a stronger model usually cuts the rejection rate faster than editing prompts does
The worker briefs and acceptance criteria, since a high rejection rate usually means the task or the criteria are unclear
The planner's decomposition, adding a second verifier pass so borderline output gets a tie-breaking judgment
questions.explanation: High rejection usually points to unclear briefs or criteria, so read those before changing anything else. Loosening the verifier or adding a tie-breaker treats the symptom, and a bigger worker model spends money before the task is even well defined.

questions.question: Your agent's tool surface has grown to 60 tools and accuracy is falling. Best structural fix?
options: Rewrite all 60 descriptions with examples and add a tool-selection few-shot block to the system prompt
Move to a larger model tier, since tool selection accuracy scales with capability at this tool count
Order the tool list by call frequency so the most used tools appear first in the model's context
Group tools behind fewer well-scoped interfaces or route to specialist subagents with small tool sets
questions.explanation: Large flat tool sets degrade selection, so partition them. Better descriptions help at the margin but leave 60 candidates competing for every call, and ordering by frequency does nothing for the rare tools that cause most of the errors.

questions.question: A long-running agent must survive process restarts. What is required?
options: Durable state: the plan, progress, and pending tool results persisted outside the process
Idempotent tools, so that re-running the task from the first turn after a restart produces the same result
A supervisor that restarts the process and re-sends the original request with a note to continue where it left off
A larger context window so the full history fits when the process reloads the last transcript
questions.explanation: Durability lives outside the process: persist the plan, progress, and pending results so a restart resumes rather than restarts. Idempotent tools make a full re-run safe but still throw away all the work, and a note to continue gives the new process nothing to continue from.

questions.question: Which design keeps a coordinator's context from growing without bound over hundreds of subtasks?
options: Restart the coordinator on a fixed cadence and hand the new instance the last user message plus the task list
Subagents return compact results; the coordinator keeps a structured ledger and compacts periodically
Each subagent appends its full transcript so the coordinator can re-check work without re-running it
Stream subagent output straight to the user and keep the coordinator stateless between subtasks
questions.explanation: Compact returns plus a ledger keep the coordinator's context proportional to the work that matters. Scheduled restarts lose progress each time, and a stateless coordinator cannot sequence or reconcile hundreds of dependent subtasks.

questions.question: You need a prompt that behaves the same across model upgrades. What practice helps most?
options: A detailed persona and tone section, since style stability is what users notice most across model versions
Explicit, testable instructions plus a golden eval set that runs on every model change
Pin the model version in config and treat any upgrade as a new project with a freshly written prompt
Few-shot examples drawn from the previous model's best outputs so the new model imitates them
questions.explanation: Specificity plus evals: explicit instructions transfer, and the eval set tells you where they did not. Examples from the old model anchor the new one to old behavior including its mistakes, and rewriting from scratch per upgrade guarantees drift.

questions.question: An MCP server exposes tools with side effects to several agents. What must the server enforce itself?
options: Authorization per caller and idempotency on side-effecting operations
Structured logging of every call with the caller's agent id so misuse can be traced after the fact
Rate limits per client and a global concurrency cap so no single agent can exhaust the backend
Tool descriptions that state the side effects clearly so calling agents gate them appropriately
questions.explanation: Servers cannot rely on callers: authorization and idempotency have to be enforced where the side effect happens. Logging and rate limits are worth having but detect or throttle misuse rather than prevent it, and descriptions only work if every caller honors them.

questions.question: Which caching strategy suits a system with a large stable policy document and per-user variable content?
options: Cache each user's full conversation as its own prefix so that repeat visits hit the cache
Place the user content first so the model sees it before the policy, then cache the policy block
Skip caching, since per-user variation means most requests miss and the cache write premium is wasted
Cache the policy document as the prefix and put per-user content after the breakpoint
questions.explanation: Stable prefix cached, variable suffix uncached. Putting user content first breaks the shared prefix for every request, and per-user caches only pay off for the rare user who returns within the cache lifetime.

questions.question: An agent's plan step produces good plans but execution drifts. What is the architectural response?
options: Drop the separate planning step and let a single stronger model plan and execute in one pass
Increase the planning depth so the plan covers more of the edge cases the executor might wander into during long runs
Make the plan an explicit artifact that execution checks against, with a review step when it deviates
Add a retry at the end of execution that reruns the task when the output fails validation
questions.explanation: Plans are useful when execution is held to them, so make the plan a checked artifact. A deeper plan does not stop the executor from ignoring it, and an end-of-run retry discovers the drift only after all the cost has been spent.

questions.question: Which of these is the right place for a hard spending limit on an agent?
options: The system prompt, as a stated token budget the model tracks and stops at on its own
The tool descriptions, with a cost annotation so the model prefers cheaper calls
The runtime: a budget enforced by the loop or a hook that stops the run
The billing dashboard, with an alert to the on-call engineer at 80% of budget
questions.explanation: Enforce budgets in code, where they cannot be forgotten or reasoned around. A budget in the prompt is a request the model may not honor, and a dashboard alert arrives after the money is spent.

questions.question: A system uses one prompt for five customer segments and quality varies by segment. Approach?
options: Route by segment to specialized prompts and evaluate each route separately
Expand the single prompt with a section per segment so the model applies the right guidance
Add few-shot examples from the weakest segment until its scores match the others
Raise the model tier for all segments, since the variance reflects a capability limit
questions.explanation: Routing plus per-route evals lets each segment be tuned and measured on its own. Segment sections in one prompt still compete for attention and are evaluated as a blend, and examples from the weakest segment can shift quality on the others.

questions.question: What is the main risk of letting subagents spawn their own subagents without limits?
options: Duplicate work, since sibling subagents cannot see each other's results without a shared store
Loss of detail, since each level summarizes upward and precision degrades with depth
Rate limit exhaustion at the API layer, which the provider handles with backoff in any case
Unbounded cost and untraceable behavior, so depth and fan-out need caps
questions.explanation: Cap recursion and fan-out: without limits, cost and behavior both become impossible to bound or trace. Duplicate work and summarization loss are real but bounded problems; unbounded spawning has no ceiling at all.

questions.question: A retrieval-augmented agent returns confident answers from stale documents. Fix?
options: A larger retrieval window so that newer documents are more likely to appear among the results
Freshness metadata in the index, ranking or filtering by recency, and surfacing dates in the answer
A reranker tuned on relevance so the most on-topic chunk wins regardless of its age
A system prompt instruction telling the model to hedge when it is unsure whether a source is current
questions.explanation: Freshness is a retrieval property: index the dates, rank on them, and show them. A relevance reranker will happily pick an on-topic but outdated chunk, and a hedging instruction cannot tell the model which sources are stale.

questions.question: Which is the strongest reason to keep tool results out of the system prompt?
options: The system prompt is for instructions; data belongs in turns so it stays data and can be managed
Prompt caching only applies to the system prompt, so adding data there invalidates the cache
System prompts have a hard length cap that tool results would exceed on most real tasks
Tool results in the system prompt are billed at a higher rate than the same tokens in messages
questions.explanation: Instructions and data stay separate: data in turns can be truncated, compacted, and treated as untrusted. Caching applies to any stable prefix, not only the system prompt, and there is no separate billing rate or special cap for system prompt tokens.

questions.question: When should an architect prefer a deterministic function over a model call inside a workflow?
options: Only when latency matters, since a model call on a small tier is comparable in cost
Whenever the logic is fully specifiable; code is cheaper, faster, and testable
Only for arithmetic and date math, where model error rates are known to be high
When the step is on the critical path, keeping model calls for background work
questions.explanation: Do not spend a model on what code can do: anything fully specifiable belongs in code regardless of where it sits in the workflow. Restricting this to math or to the critical path leaves plenty of deterministic logic paying model cost and variance.

questions.question: A Claude Code deployment across a 200-engineer org needs consistent behavior. Which lever scales?
options: A central prompt-engineering team that reviews a sample of each engineer's session transcripts weekly
An internal wiki with recommended prompts and a Slack channel for questions
Each engineer's user-level settings and memory, tuned during an onboarding workshop
Checked-in CLAUDE.md, shared skills, hooks, and project-scoped MCP config
questions.explanation: Configuration in the repo scales: every engineer gets the same instructions, skills, hooks, and MCP servers on checkout. Wikis and workshops depend on people remembering, and per-user settings drift the moment someone edits theirs.

questions.question: What should an evaluator in an evaluator-optimizer loop output?
options: A corrected version of the output, so the loop converges in one step instead of several
A single numeric score, keeping the evaluator cheap and its output easy to threshold
A structured verdict against explicit criteria with specific feedback the generator can act on
A pass or fail flag plus the full reasoning trace so that humans can audit the decision later without re-running it
questions.explanation: Actionable, structured feedback is what lets the generator improve. A bare score gives it nothing to act on, and a rewritten output turns the evaluator into a second generator with no independent check.

questions.question: Which context strategy suits an agent that reads thousands of tickets a day?
options: Load the full day's tickets into one long-context call so the model can spot cross-ticket patterns
One agent per ticket with no shared state, relying on the ticket system for any aggregation
Process in batches with per-batch summaries and a rolling state document
Embed all tickets and let the agent retrieve as needed with no persistent working state
questions.explanation: Batch, summarize, roll state: bounded context per call plus a carried summary. One giant call is expensive and degrades with length, and per-ticket agents with no shared state cannot see patterns across tickets at all.

questions.question: A team asks whether to expose a tool as one call with many options or several narrow tools. Guidance?
options: Prefer narrow, clearly described tools; combine only when the model routinely needs them together
Prefer one tool with an options schema, since fewer tools keep the definitions block small
Prefer many tools in every case, since each extra tool adds a few tokens and selection is cheap
Mirror the backend REST endpoints one to one so that the mapping between each tool and its API call is obvious to maintainers
questions.explanation: Narrow tools select better and are easier to describe and test. One tool with many modes hides the choice inside a schema the model fills in less reliably, and mirroring REST endpoints optimizes for the API's shape rather than the model's.

questions.question: Which artifact should exist before an agent is allowed to act on production systems?
options: A passing eval run above the launch threshold on the current golden set
A risk register listing each action, its blast radius, its gate, and its rollback
A signed change request from the system owner covering the agent's service account
A load test showing the agent stays within the production API's rate limits
questions.explanation: Risks, gates, rollbacks: the register is what makes every production action deliberate. A passing eval says the agent is usually right, not what happens when it is wrong, and a signed change request records approval without defining the controls.

questions.question: An audit asks why the agent took a specific action last month. What lets you answer?
options: The prompt version deployed that month and the eval results attached to its release
The agent's memory store, which records the facts it had learned by that date
A replay of the request on today's system with the same inputs to reproduce the decision
Per-call logs of inputs, tool calls, results, and decisions, retained per policy
questions.explanation: Auditability is logging plus retention: the record of what actually happened. A replay on today's system produces today's decision, not last month's, and the prompt version explains the rules rather than the specific action.

questions.question: What is a kill switch in an agent system?
options: An operator control that halts the system immediately, independent of the model
A tool the model calls when it detects it is outside policy, ending the run
A per-run timeout that stops any task exceeding its expected duration
A feature flag that routes new requests to a fallback and lets in-flight runs finish
questions.explanation: Operator-controlled and model-independent: it has to work when the model is the thing misbehaving. A tool the model calls depends on the model noticing, and a flag that lets in-flight runs finish is exactly what a kill switch must not do.

questions.question: A client wants the agent to use customer data from another client's engagement to improve results. Response?
options: Agree if the other client's contract permits data reuse for service improvement
Anonymize the records and proceed, since de-identified data is no longer client data
Refuse; client data isolation is a governance boundary, not an optimization trade-off
Use the other client's data only to build the eval set, not in production prompts
questions.explanation: Isolation is a boundary, not a dial. Anonymization is the strongest distractor, but de-identified records still originate from the other client's engagement and re-identification risk remains; using them for evals crosses the same line.

questions.question: How should personal data be handled in prompts where possible?
options: Included in full so the model has context, with zero data retention configured on the API
Minimized or redacted, with only what the task needs
Encrypted inside the prompt text so the model processes it without seeing plaintext
Duplicated in the system prompt and the user turn so that retrieval cannot miss a field
questions.explanation: Minimize what enters the prompt: redact or omit anything the task does not need. Zero retention limits what the provider keeps but not what your own logs and traces capture, and a model cannot reason over ciphertext.

questions.question: Which change to an agent requires a fresh risk review?
options: Changing the model tier used for a read-only summarization step
Rewriting a tool description to improve selection accuracy
Raising the retry count on a read-only search tool from two to three
Adding a tool that can send, delete, or pay
questions.explanation: New capabilities with side effects change the risk profile. A model tier change on a read-only step is worth an eval run, but it does not add any action the agent could not already take.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a staged rollout for an agent change?
options: Limiting blast radius while monitoring real behavior before full exposure
Reducing eval cost by testing on live traffic instead of maintaining a golden set
Meeting the launch date while the remaining tests continue to run in parallel
Collecting user feedback on the interface before committing to the design
questions.explanation: Contain and observe: a stage limits who is affected while you watch real behavior. Stages complement evals rather than replace them, and using a rollout to skip tests puts real users in the role of the test set.

questions.question: A CFO asks 'what does this agent cost us per month and what happens if it breaks?' The right answer includes:
options: Model names, token counts per task, and the prompt caching rate that keeps the monthly bill down
Cost per task and per month, failure modes, how they are detected, and time to recover
A live demo plus a commitment to SLA-backed uptime from the model provider
Total tokens per month and the provider's published availability figures
questions.explanation: Cost, failure, recovery, in the CFO's units. Token counts and caching rates are inputs to cost rather than the cost, and the provider's uptime says nothing about what your agent does when it fails.

questions.question: Which metric set belongs on an agent's monthly review?
options: Prompt versions shipped, eval pass rate, and model release notes reviewed
Token volume, cache hit rate, and API error rate by endpoint
Completion rate, quality score, cost per task, incidents, and time to recover
User count, sessions per user, and feature requests logged
questions.explanation: Operational outcomes are what a monthly review should track. Token volume and cache hit rate are engineering diagnostics, useful for tuning but not for judging whether the agent is doing its job.

questions.question: A stakeholder wants a feature that the evals show is unreliable. Your move?
options: Ship it behind a feature flag so that it can be turned off quickly if users begin to complain about it
Decline the request and escalate to the sponsor with the eval numbers attached
Raise the eval threshold and ship once a stronger model tier clears it
Show the eval results, state the risk, and propose a gated rollout or scope reduction
questions.explanation: Evidence plus options keeps the decision with the stakeholder and the risk visible. A feature flag makes users the detectors of a failure you already know about, and escalating without options turns a design conversation into a standoff.

questions.question: How should prompt changes be communicated to stakeholders of a production system?
options: As versioned releases with eval results and a rollback plan
In the monthly review, summarized as the number of prompt edits made
Only when the change alters user-visible behavior, via the release notes
Through the change ticket that the engineer files when editing the prompt
questions.explanation: Treat prompts as releases: version, evidence, rollback. Release notes only for visible changes miss the prompt edits that quietly shift quality, and an engineer's ticket is a record rather than a communication.

questions.question: Which event should trigger a lifecycle review of an agent system?
options: A quarter end, so that reviews line up with the budget cycle
A change in the on-call rotation or the team that owns the agent
A model upgrade, a change in tool capabilities, or a shift in the task's inputs
A new release of the agent framework or SDK that the runtime uses, since dependencies change behavior
questions.explanation: Change in model, tools, or inputs is what changes how the agent behaves, so that is what should trigger the review. Calendar reviews are fine as a floor, and an SDK release matters only if it changes one of those three.

questions.question: A production agent's accuracy dropped after a tool provider changed its response format. What should have caught it?
options: Pinning the provider's API version in the client so that format changes could not reach production
Contract tests on tool responses plus a scheduled eval that alerts on drift
A larger eval set run before each of your own releases, covering more of the tool paths
Schema validation in the tool wrapper that coerces unexpected fields to safe defaults
questions.explanation: External dependencies change on their own schedule; contract tests and scheduled evals detect it before users do. Pre-release evals only run when you ship, so a change on the provider's side slips through, and silent coercion hides the break instead of surfacing it.

questions.question: Which design keeps a multi-tenant agent from leaking one customer's context into another's?
options: Per-tenant context, memory, and tool credentials, with tenant id enforced in every tool call
A system prompt instruction that names the current tenant and forbids any reference to others
Random session ids per conversation so that contexts cannot be guessed across tenants
A shared memory store partitioned by a tenant tag that the model includes in each query
questions.explanation: Isolation is enforced in the runtime and tools, not requested in prose. A tenant tag the model supplies is the strongest distractor, but it relies on the model getting the tag right on every query, which is exactly the failure you are guarding against.

questions.question: A coordinator agent spends most of its tokens re-reading subagent transcripts. Fix?
options: A larger context window on the coordinator so that full transcripts fit without truncation or summarization
Fewer, larger subagents so there are fewer transcripts for the coordinator to read
Prompt caching on each transcript so that repeated reads cost less per token
Subagents return structured summaries; the coordinator keeps a ledger instead of transcripts
questions.explanation: Structured returns keep the coordinator lean and its decisions grounded in what matters. Caching lowers the price of re-reading but not the context consumed, and fewer subagents just concentrates the same transcript volume.

questions.question: How should an architect decide between extended thinking and a second verification call?
options: Extended thinking by default, since it keeps the workflow to one call and one bill
A verification call by default, since a second independent pass catches more errors
By measuring: run both on the eval set and compare accuracy, cost, and latency for that task
By task type: extended thinking for reasoning-heavy tasks, verification for extraction and formatting work
questions.explanation: Empirical comparison on the task decides; both techniques have cases where they win. Rules of thumb by task type are a starting hypothesis, not a decision, and either default leaves the cheaper or more accurate option untested.

questions.question: Which practice makes a prompt library maintainable across a large team?
options: A shared document where any engineer can edit, with a weekly review of the accumulated diff
Ownership per prompt, versioning, an eval per prompt, and a change process
A single senior owner for the whole library who personally approves every change
A freeze on all prompts outside a monthly release window, with edits batched
questions.explanation: Prompts are production assets; manage them as such, with an owner, history, and a test per prompt. A single approver becomes the bottleneck and still has no eval to check against, and a freeze slows change without making it safer.

questions.question: What is the failure mode of caching aggressively in an agent with per-user personalization?
options: Personal content placed before the breakpoint defeats the cache, or a shared prefix built wrong leaks user data
Cached prefixes go stale, so users keep seeing policy text from before the last deployment
Cache writes cost more than reads, so low-repeat traffic pays a premium for no benefit
The cache lifetime expires in the middle of a conversation, forcing a full uncached re-read of the prefix on the very next turn
questions.explanation: Cache boundaries must respect data ownership and stability: personal data before the breakpoint kills the hit rate, and a shared prefix assembled from user data can leak across users. A cache expiring mid-conversation costs money but exposes nothing.

questions.question: A client wants the agent to remember everything forever. Your design answer?
options: Append every transcript to a vector index and retrieve the top matches into each prompt
Keep full transcripts in the prompt and rely on a long-context model tier to hold them
Store durable facts and decisions in a memory store with retention rules; load what a task needs
Decline memory entirely and require the user to restate context at the start of each session
questions.explanation: Selective, governed memory beats hoarding: facts and decisions with retention rules, loaded on demand. Indexing every transcript keeps everything forever with no governance, which is the request restated rather than a design.

questions.question: An MCP server is shared by several teams' agents and performance degrades under load. First architectural move?
options: Switch transports from HTTP to stdio so that each agent gets its own dedicated server process
Add a second server instance and split the teams by name across the two
Reduce the number of tools exposed so each call carries less schema overhead
Rate limits and per-client quotas on the server, plus caching of read-heavy resources
questions.explanation: Shared services need quotas and caching so one heavy client cannot degrade the rest. A second instance doubles capacity once without addressing the fairness problem, and a per-agent stdio process shifts the load onto whatever backend the server calls.

questions.question: Which signal tells you a workflow step should become a model call rather than code?
options: Its inputs are unstructured or ambiguous and rules keep failing on edge cases
It runs on every request, so a model call's consistency matters more than its cost
It is slow in code, and a small model tier would return an answer faster
It is the step users complain about most, regardless of what the complaints say
