questions.explanation: Ambiguity is where models earn their cost. A step that runs on every request is the last place to add model latency and variance, and user complaints about a deterministic step usually mean a bug rather than a need for judgment.

questions.question: How do you keep a 60-tool integration surface manageable for an agent?
options: Give the model all 60 with a routing table in the system prompt that maps each user intent to the right tool
Partition tools by task into specialist subagents or dynamic tool loading, each with a small relevant set
Merge related tools into a few generic ones with a mode parameter that selects the behavior
Sort the tool list by usage and drop the bottom 40, since rarely used tools add noise
questions.explanation: Small, relevant tool sets per context is what keeps selection accurate. Generic tools with a mode parameter move the choice into an argument the model fills in less reliably, and dropping the rare tools removes capability rather than managing it.

questions.question: What belongs in the audit record for an agent action that changed a customer's data?
options: The before and after state of the record plus the model version and prompt version that produced the change
The final state of the record and the user id of the session owner
The full conversation transcript, stored against the ticket for that customer
Who or what triggered it, the inputs, the tool call and result, the approval if any, and a timestamp
questions.explanation: The record has to make the action reconstructable: trigger, inputs, call, result, approval, time. Before and after states show what changed but not why or who allowed it, and a raw transcript is hard to query and often contains data the audit should not.

questions.question: A regulator asks how the agent avoids discriminatory outcomes in a decision-support use case. What must exist?
options: A disclaimer in the output stating that the recommendation is advisory only
A system prompt instructing the model to ignore protected attributes when reasoning
Documented bias evaluation, human review on decisions, and monitoring with defined thresholds
Use of the largest available model tier, which carries the strongest fairness training
questions.explanation: Evidence, oversight, monitoring: a regulator wants to see measurement and controls, not intent. A prompt instruction is the strongest distractor, but it is unverifiable on its own and proxies for protected attributes pass straight through it.

questions.question: Which is the right response to discovering the agent logged full credit card numbers?
options: Stop the logging, purge the records, assess exposure, and add redaction with tests
Restrict log access to the security team and shorten the retention window to seven days
Encrypt the log store at rest and add the finding to the next quarterly risk review
Add redaction to the logger and let the existing records age out under the retention policy
questions.explanation: Contain, remediate, prevent. Adding redaction going forward is the strongest distractor, but leaving the existing numbers in place until they age out means the exposure continues, and restricting access does not remove the data.

questions.question: What is a sensible policy for agent access to production databases?
options: Full read access on the primary with writes blocked at the network layer
Reads through scoped views by default; writes through audited, gated operations
A dedicated agent role that mirrors the application's service account so the agent can do what the app does
No database access; the agent files tickets that a human executes by hand
questions.explanation: Scoped reads, gated writes. Full read on the primary exposes every column including the ones the agent has no reason to see, and mirroring the application role grants the agent the app's full write surface without the app's business logic in front of it.

questions.question: How should an architect treat a model's refusal behavior in a regulated workflow?
options: As the primary control, documented in the compliance file as the enforcement mechanism
As a signal to tune away with the system prompt so the workflow completes reliably
As a reason to route the refused requests to a less restrictive model tier
As one safety layer among several, with policy enforced in code and review regardless
questions.explanation: Model refusals are one layer; policy is enforced in code, gates, and human review regardless of what the model does. Treating refusals as the primary control leaves compliance resting on behavior that changes with every model version.

questions.question: What should a change-management process require before an agent's tool set expands?
options: A code review of the tool wrapper and a passing run of the existing eval set
Approval from the tool's system owner and an updated tool description
A risk review of the new capabilities, updated gates, tests, and a staged rollout
A load test of the new tool and a rate limit configured on the MCP server
questions.explanation: Capability changes are risk changes. A code review plus the existing evals is the strongest distractor, but the existing evals were written for the old tool set and say nothing about what the new tool can do wrong.

questions.question: Which incident-response element is specific to agent systems?
options: An on-call rotation with paging tied to error rate and latency alerts on the agent service
The ability to halt autonomous actions immediately and replay decisions from logs
A blameless postmortem held within a fixed window after resolution
A public status page updated while the incident is in progress
questions.explanation: Kill switch plus replay: an agent can keep acting during an incident, and understanding what it decided needs the decision log. Paging, postmortems, and status pages apply to any production system.

questions.question: A client asks for a single number: 'how accurate is it?' What do you give them?
options: The eval pass rate as a single percentage, so the client has the number they asked for
Accuracy on a defined eval set with the date, the failure categories, and what happens on failure
A range spanning the best and worst eval runs from the past quarter
A comparison to human accuracy on the same task, drawn from the client's own quality assurance records for the past year
questions.explanation: Numbers with definitions and consequences. A bare percentage will be quoted without the eval set it came from, and a human comparison is useful context but does not tell the client what the failures look like or what happens when one occurs.

questions.question: How do you set expectations for an agent's first month in production?
options: A commitment to the eval accuracy figure as a production SLA from day one
A soft launch to a friendly team with no metrics until usage has settled down
Full autonomy on the low-risk tasks from day one and a promise to review the remaining tasks after 30 days
A staged plan with metrics, human review levels, and the criteria for expanding autonomy
questions.explanation: Stages, metrics, criteria: expectations are set by saying what will be measured and what earns more autonomy. Promising the eval figure as an SLA ignores that production inputs differ from the eval set, and a soft launch with no metrics learns nothing.

questions.question: A stakeholder wants to skip evals to hit a launch date. Your position as the architect?
options: Agree, provided the stakeholder signs a written risk acceptance and the full evals run during the week after launch
Ship with production monitoring in place of evals, since live traffic is the more realistic test
Explain the risk concretely, offer a reduced-scope launch that keeps the eval gate, and document the decision
Hold the launch until the full eval suite passes, whatever that does to the date
questions.explanation: Trade scope, not the safety gate. A signed risk acceptance is the strongest distractor, since it records the decision, but it still puts an untested system in front of users, and monitoring finds failures after they have happened.

questions.question: Which artifact keeps a long-running agent engagement healthy across team changes?
options: A living runbook: architecture, gates, evals, known failure modes, and on-call procedures
The original proposal and statement of work, kept current through change orders
The chat history between the team and the client, archived and searchable
Recorded handover sessions from each departing engineer, stored with the project
questions.explanation: Written operational knowledge that is kept current is what survives turnover. Handover recordings capture one person's view at one moment and go stale, and the statement of work describes what was promised rather than how the system runs.

questions.question: When a model provider announces a deprecation, what is the lifecycle response?
options: Switch to the successor in production at once, since the provider has already validated it
Plan the migration: run evals on the successor, compare, canary, cut over, and update docs
Stay on the deprecated model until the retirement date to avoid churn, then switch
Freeze the agent's scope and run both models in parallel for the foreseeable future
questions.explanation: Planned migration with evidence. Waiting until the retirement date is the strongest distractor, since it avoids churn, but it turns a scheduled migration into a forced one with no time left to fix what the evals find.

questions.question: How should success be reported to executives for an agent that handles support tickets?
options: Tokens per day, cache hit rate, and average latency per response
The number of tickets the agent touched, the average handling time, and the uptime of the service
Prompt versions shipped and the eval pass rate per release
Resolution rate, customer satisfaction, cost per ticket, escalation rate, and incidents, trended
questions.explanation: Business outcomes, trended, are what executives can act on. Tickets touched and uptime describe activity rather than results, and eval pass rate is an engineering signal that says nothing about customers.

questions.question: A retailer wants Claude to answer product questions from a 40,000-document catalog that changes daily. Which architecture fits?
options: Fine-tune a model on the catalog nightly
Load the catalog into the system prompt
An autonomous agent that browses the public website

questions.question: After a re-index, your retrieval system returns semantically similar but commercially wrong products. Which investigation comes first?
options: The generation prompt
The model version
The user interface

questions.question: An agent used by 300 employees exposes 45 tools across eight systems. Selection quality is degrading. What is the architectural response?
options: Shorten all tool descriptions
Merge tools into a few multi-mode tools
Replace the agent with a larger model

questions.question: Which evaluation design best fits a summarization feature where quality is subjective?
options: Exact match against reference summaries
Average output length compared to references
User thumbs-up counts alone

questions.question: Before a prompt change reaches all users, what is the disciplined sequence?
options: Ship it and monitor complaints
Team vote followed by rollout
Rollout with a feedback form

questions.question: A hospital system requires that protected health information never reach the model provider, while clinicians need free-text search. Which design satisfies both?
options: A policy instructing clinicians not to type identifiers
A system prompt instructing the model to disregard PHI
Restricting the feature to structured queries only

questions.question: Which is the correct application of human-in-the-loop review at scale?
options: Review every output regardless of risk
Review a fixed 10% sample chosen at random
Review only what users complain about

questions.question: An executive sponsor demands a single accuracy number for a system whose performance varies sharply by document type. What does a competent architect present?
options: The highest observed number
A refusal to quantify
An average weighted to look favorable

questions.question: Your design must satisfy GDPR for EU customer data. Which requirement most directly shapes the architecture?
options: Response latency targets
The choice of programming language
The number of model providers

questions.question: Which is the correct reason to prefer a workflow over an agent for a document intake process?
options: Workflows are always more accurate
Agents cannot process documents
Workflows use less context

questions.question: An application sends an identical 12,000-token policy preamble on every request. Which optimization addresses both latency and cost?
options: Splitting the preamble across two requests
Summarizing the preamble with the model at request time
Moving the preamble into a few-shot block

questions.question: What belongs in an architecture decision record for a Claude system?
options: The final design only
The team members involved
The implementation timeline

questions.question: Observability for a production agent should capture which of the following to make incidents diagnosable?
options: Final outputs only
Aggregate latency metrics only
User feedback only

questions.question: A partner team wants to adopt your Claude Code setup. What makes adoption durable rather than a one-time handoff?
options: A recorded walkthrough
A shared chat channel
Individual coaching sessions

questions.question: Which change best reduces risk in an agent that can both read and modify production records?
options: Logging modifications for later review
Requiring a longer system prompt about caution
Running the agent during business hours only
